templates.pattern: A radioactive source has an initial activity of [A0] Bq and a half life of [THALF] years. Calculate the activity after [TIME] years in Bq.
templates.explanation:
Activity A = A₀ × (0.5)^(t ÷ T½)
= [A0] × (0.5)^([TIME] ÷ [THALF])
= [A0] × (0.5)^[TIME/THALF]
= [RESULT] Bq

This formula works for any time — not just whole numbers of half lives. The exponent t/T½ tells us how many half lives have elapsed.

templates.pattern: A radioactive sample has an initial mass of [M0] g and a half life of [THALF] years. Calculate the mass remaining after [TIME] years in grams.
templates.explanation:
Mass remaining M = M₀ × (0.5)^(t ÷ T½)
= [M0] × (0.5)^([TIME] ÷ [THALF])
= [M0] × (0.5)^[TIME/THALF]
= [RESULT] g

This continuous decay formula gives the mass at any time t. It is the same exponential relationship as for activity.

templates.pattern: A radioactive isotope has a decay constant of [LAM] × 10⁻³ per second. Calculate the half life of the isotope in seconds.
templates.explanation:
Half life T½ = 0.693 ÷ λ
= 0.693 ÷ ([LAM] × 10⁻³)
= 693 ÷ [LAM]
= [RESULT] s

The decay constant and half life are inversely related. A large decay constant means a short half life and rapid decay.

templates.pattern: A radioactive source contains [N] × 10¹⁰ atoms and has a decay constant of [LAM] × 10⁻³ per second. Calculate the activity of the source in Bq.
templates.explanation:
Activity A = λ × N
= [LAM] × 10⁻³ × [N] × 10¹⁰
= [LAM] × [N] × 10⁷
= [RESULT] Bq

Activity is directly proportional to both the number of radioactive atoms and the decay constant. A source with more atoms or a larger decay constant has a higher activity.

templates.pattern: A photon has a frequency of [F] × 10¹⁴ Hz. Calculate the energy of the photon in joules. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)
templates.explanation:
Photon energy E = hf
= 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × [F] × 10¹⁴
= 6.63 × [F] × 10⁻²⁰
= [RESULT] J

The energy of a photon is directly proportional to its frequency. Higher frequency radiation such as gamma rays carries more energy per photon than lower frequency radiation such as radio waves.

templates.pattern: An electron of mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg moves at [V] × 10⁶ m/s. Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of the electron in metres. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)
templates.explanation:
de Broglie wavelength λ = h ÷ (mv)
= 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ ÷ (9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × [V] × 10⁶)
= 6.63 ÷ (9.11 × [V] × 10³) nm range
= [RESULT] m

The de Broglie wavelength shows that particles have wave properties. Electrons have wavelengths similar to atomic spacings which is why electron diffraction is used to study crystal structures.

templates.pattern: Light of frequency [F] × 10¹⁴ Hz falls on a metal surface with a work function of [PHI] × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons in joules. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)
templates.explanation:
Maximum KE = hf − φ
= 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × [F] × 10¹⁴ − [PHI] × 10⁻¹⁹
= [6.63*F] × 10⁻²⁰ − [PHI] × 10⁻¹⁹
= [RESULT] J

The work function φ is the minimum energy needed to release an electron from the surface. Any extra photon energy becomes kinetic energy of the photoelectron.

templates.pattern: Light of frequency [F] × 10¹⁴ Hz causes photoelectric emission from a metal with work function [PHI] × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Calculate the stopping potential in volts. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
templates.explanation:
Stopping potential eV₀ = hf − φ
V₀ = (hf − φ) ÷ e
= (6.63 × [F] × 10⁻²⁰ − [PHI] × 10⁻¹⁹) ÷ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹
= [RESULT] V

The stopping potential is the minimum reverse voltage needed to stop all photoelectrons. It directly measures the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons.

templates.pattern: A metal has a work function of [PHI] × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Calculate the threshold frequency for photoelectric emission in Hz. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)
templates.explanation:
Threshold frequency f₀ = φ ÷ h
= [PHI] × 10⁻¹⁹ ÷ 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴
= [PHI] ÷ 6.63 × 10¹⁵
= [RESULT] Hz

Below the threshold frequency no electrons are emitted regardless of intensity. This proves light consists of photons — particles of energy hf.

templates.pattern: An electron in an atom falls from a higher energy level to a lower one. The wavelength of the emitted photon is [LAM] × 10⁻⁷ m. Calculate the energy of the emitted photon in joules. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)
templates.explanation:
Photon energy E = hc ÷ λ
= 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3 × 10⁸ ÷ ([LAM] × 10⁻⁷)
= 19.89 × 10⁻²⁶ ÷ [LAM] × 10⁻⁷
= [RESULT] J

When an electron transitions to a lower energy level it releases a photon. The wavelength of this photon gives spectral lines unique to each element — this is the basis of spectroscopy.
